Forms of government include monarchy, aristocracy and democracy (Aristotle's classification); democratic and dictatorial; unitary and federal; parliamentary and presidential.

Government is temporary and changes through elections or other means, while the state is permanent. Government is the visible agent; the state is an abstract concept. Government's functions include protection of life and property, maintenance of law and order, defence, foreign relations, collection of taxes and welfare activities such as education, health and social security. In modern democracies, the term 'governance' refers to the broader process of decision-making involving government, the private sector and civil society.
A nation is a community whose members share a sense of collective identity, often based on history, culture or political belonging.

The word 'nation' comes from the Latin 'natio', meaning birth or race. A nation is a group of people who share a sense of common identity and belonging, based on factors such as common descent, language, religion, culture, history, territory and political aspirations. Ernest Renan ('What is a Nation?', 1882) described the nation as a 'daily plebiscite' - a shared will to live together, based on common memories and sacrifices. Benedict Anderson called nations 'imagined communities', created by print and shared media.

No single factor is essential: Switzerland has several languages, India has many religions and languages, yet both are nations. A nationality is sometimes used for a cultural group that has not yet achieved statehood. Nationalism is the ideology that a nation should have its own state and that loyalty to the nation is paramount. Nationalism can be liberating (anti-colonial movements) or aggressive (fascism, chauvinism).
A nation-state is a state in which political territory and a strong national identity broadly coincide.

The nation-state became the dominant form of political organisation after the Peace of Westphalia (1648) and the French Revolution (1789), which popularised the idea that sovereignty belongs to the nation. The principle of national self-determination (Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points, 1918) led to the creation of new nation-states after the First World War, and decolonisation after 1945 created many more.

Few states are purely mono-national; most contain several ethnic, linguistic or religious groups, making them multinational states (for example, India, the UK, Canada). This creates challenges of accommodating minorities and demands for autonomy or secession. Globalisation, supranational organisations (the EU), migration and transnational identities have also challenged the nation-state model.
Citizenship is legal and political membership in a state and includes rights as well as duties.

Citizenship is full membership of a state, giving civil, political and social rights and imposing duties. Aristotle defined a citizen as one who shares in the administration of justice and in holding office. T. H. Marshall ('Citizenship and Social Class', 1950) traced the development of civil rights (eighteenth century), political rights (nineteenth century) and social rights (twentieth century) in Britain.

Citizenship can be acquired by birth (jus soli - the law of soil; jus sanguinis - the law of blood), registration, naturalisation, incorporation of territory and marriage in some countries; it can be lost by renunciation, termination or deprivation. In India, Articles 5-11 of the Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955 (amended several times, including the controversial Citizenship Amendment Act, 2019) govern citizenship; India provides single citizenship. Good citizenship requires education, awareness, tolerance, participation and the performance of duties.
Liberty means freedom from unnecessary restrictions and the ability to act and develop.

Liberty has two sides: negative (absence of restraint) and positive (presence of opportunities). Types include natural liberty (the freedom of the state of nature), civil liberty (rights under law, such as freedom of speech, movement and religion), political liberty (the right to vote and participate), economic liberty (freedom from want and exploitation) and national liberty (independence of the nation).

Liberty is limited by law to protect the freedom of others; Locke said, 'where there is no law, there is no freedom'. In India, Articles 19-22 guarantee freedoms of speech, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession, and protection of life and personal liberty, subject to reasonable restrictions. Safeguards of liberty include democracy, constitutional rights, independent judiciary, rule of law, separation of powers, a free press and active citizens.
Equality means recognition of equal moral worth and fair political and social status.

Equality means the absence of special privileges and the provision of equal opportunities for all to develop themselves (Laski). It does not mean identical treatment, since people have different needs and abilities; sometimes unequal treatment (affirmative action) is needed to achieve real equality. Types include natural, legal (equality before law and equal protection of laws), social, political, economic and international equality.

In India, the Constitution guarantees equality before law (Article 14), prohibition of discrimination (Article 15), equality of opportunity in public employment (Article 16), abolition of untouchability (Article 17) and abolition of titles (Article 18). Reservations for SCs, STs and OBCs and the EWS quota (103rd Amendment, 2019) aim at substantive equality.
Justice concerns fairness in rights, opportunities, duties and distribution.

Justice is the virtue of giving each person their due. Its dimensions include: legal justice (fair laws, impartial courts, equality before law and the rule of law); political justice (equal political rights, universal franchise, freedom to participate); social justice (abolition of discrimination and privileges, protection of weaker sections); and economic justice (fair distribution of wealth, removal of poverty, fair wages).

The Preamble of the Indian Constitution promises 'Justice, social, economic and political'. Directive Principles (Articles 38 and 39) seek to secure a social order based on justice, and Article 39A provides free legal aid. Theories of justice range from Plato and Aristotle to utilitarianism, Rawls, Nozick and Amartya Sen.
Rights are recognised claims or freedoms that individuals can exercise within society and the state.

Rights are essential for the full development of human personality. Characteristics: they are social (exist in society), universal (for all), recognised and protected by the state, correlated with duties, and not absolute (subject to reasonable restrictions). Kinds: moral rights (based on conscience, not enforceable by law) and legal rights (enforced by the state), which include civil rights (life, liberty, property, equality, speech, religion), political rights (vote, contest, criticise government, petition) and economic and social rights (work, fair wages, education, health).

In India, Fundamental Rights (Part III) are justiciable and include the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights and the Right to Constitutional Remedies. The Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment (1978) and became a legal right under Article 300A. The Right to Education (Article 21A) was added by the 86th Amendment (2002).
Democracy is government based on popular participation and consent.

Democracy can mean a form of government, a form of state, a social order and a way of life based on equality, liberty and fraternity. Features include government by elected representatives, accountability to the people, free and fair elections, protection of rights, majority rule with minority rights, the rule of law and peaceful change of government.

Democracy may be direct or representative, parliamentary or presidential. Merits: it is based on consent and equality, promotes political education and participation, ensures responsible and accountable government and allows peaceful change. Demerits: rule of mediocrity, high cost of elections, slow decision-making, party politics and possible tyranny of the majority. Conditions for success include education, economic equality, social harmony, a free press, strong opposition, independent judiciary and civic consciousness.
Rule of law means that government and citizens are governed by publicly known laws and that public authority is not above the law.

A. V. Dicey ('Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution', 1885) explained the rule of law in Britain through three principles: (1) supremacy of law - no person can be punished except for a distinct breach of law established in ordinary courts, and there is no arbitrary power; (2) equality before law - all persons, including officials, are subject to the ordinary law and courts; and (3) the constitution is the result of the ordinary law of the land, with rights protected by judicial decisions.

In India, Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of the laws; the Supreme Court has held that the rule of law is part of the basic structure of the Constitution (Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain, 1975). Exceptions include the immunity of the President and Governors (Article 361) and the privileges of legislators. Modern understanding of the rule of law includes fair procedure, independent judiciary, accessible justice and protection of human rights.
A constitution establishes the basic rules, institutions, powers and rights of a political system.

A constitution is the fundamental law of a state. Kinds: written (codified in a single document - India, USA) and unwritten (based on statutes, conventions and judicial decisions - UK); rigid (difficult to amend - USA) and flexible (amended like ordinary law - UK); federal and unitary. A good constitution should be clear, comprehensive, adaptable, protect rights, establish separation of powers and have an independent judiciary.

Constitutionalism means limited government - government according to constitutional rules, with checks on power to protect liberty. The Indian Constitution (adopted 26 November 1949, effective 26 January 1950) is the longest written constitution in the world, originally with 395 articles, 22 parts and 8 schedules (now about 470 articles and 12 schedules). It borrowed features from the Government of India Act 1935, the British Constitution (parliamentary system), the US Constitution (fundamental rights, judicial review), the Irish Constitution (Directive Principles), Canada (federation with strong centre) and others.
Political parties seek political power through organised participation, especially elections.

Edmund Burke defined a political party as 'a body of men united for promoting by their joint endeavours the national interest upon some particular principle in which they are all agreed'. Parties perform functions such as contesting elections, forming governments or acting as opposition, aggregating and articulating interests, making policies, recruiting leaders, educating the public and linking people and government.

Party systems: one-party (China), two-party (USA, UK traditionally), and multi-party (India, France). Maurice Duverger ('Political Parties', 1951) linked the first-past-the-post system with two-party systems ('Duverger's Law'). In India, the Election Commission recognises parties as national or state parties based on their vote share and seats. There are six national parties (as of 2023: BJP, INC, CPI(M), BSP, AAP and NPP) and many state parties. The Anti-Defection Law (Tenth Schedule, 52nd Amendment, 1985) aims to prevent defections.
Pressure groups attempt to influence public policy without normally seeking to form the government themselves.

Pressure groups (or interest groups) are organised groups that try to influence government policy in their favour. Unlike political parties, they do not contest elections or seek to form governments, and they usually focus on specific interests. Types include business groups (FICCI, CII, ASSOCHAM), trade unions (AITUC, INTUC, BMS), farmers' groups (Bharatiya Kisan Union), professional associations (Indian Medical Association, Bar Council), student groups, caste and religious groups, and issue-based or promotional groups (environmental groups, human rights groups).

Methods include lobbying, petitions, media campaigns, demonstrations, strikes, litigation (public interest litigation) and funding of parties. Pressure groups help citizens express their interests, provide expert information and act as a check on government; but they may also represent narrow interests, use undue influence (especially business groups) and sometimes cause disruption. In Mizoram, groups such as the YMA and MZP act as influential pressure groups.
Public opinion refers to the views and attitudes of citizens on public and political issues.

Public opinion is the collective view of the people on public matters. Lord Bryce defined it as 'the aggregate of the views men hold regarding matters that affect or interest the community'. Agencies that form and express public opinion include the press and electronic media, social media, political parties, pressure groups, educational institutions, religious institutions, legislatures, elections and opinion polls.

In a democracy, public opinion guides and controls government, protects rights and acts as a check on abuse of power. Sound public opinion requires literacy, a free and responsible press, freedom of speech, tolerance, economic equality and an absence of sectarian divisions. Public opinion can be manipulated through propaganda, fake news and misinformation, so media literacy is important.

sections.title: Meaning and Scope of Political Science

blocks.text:
Political Science studies politics, government, institutions, power and political behaviour. It examines how collective decisions are made and how authority is organised.

The subject includes the study of the state, government, constitutions, political parties, elections, rights and public policy. It also studies ideas such as liberty, equality and justice.

Political Science therefore combines the study of institutions with the study of political ideas and behaviour.

Meaning and nature: Political Science studies the state, government, politics and power. Aristotle is its father; modern definitions emphasise the state (Gettell, Garner), power (Lasswell, Catlin), authoritative allocation of values (Easton) and political behaviour. Whether Political Science is a science is debated: it has systematic knowledge and methods, but lacks the exactness and laboratory experiments of natural sciences. It is best described as a social science.

Scope: (1) political theory (concepts, ideologies); (2) political institutions and comparative politics (constitutions, executives, legislatures, judiciaries); (3) public administration (organisation, personnel, finance, policy); (4) international relations (diplomacy, international organisations, foreign policy); (5) political parties, pressure groups and public opinion; (6) political behaviour (voting, participation); and (7) public policy and local government. New areas include gender studies, environmental politics and globalisation.

Relations with other disciplines: history provides the material of political science (Seeley: 'History without political science has no fruit; political science without history has no root'); economics (political economy); sociology (political sociology); psychology (political psychology); philosophy (political philosophy); geography (geopolitics); and law. The study of Political Science helps develop informed, responsible citizens.

Power is the ability to influence behaviour or outcomes. Authority is a special form of power that is accepted as rightful. Legitimacy refers to the belief that an institution or ruler has a valid right to exercise authority.

A government may possess coercive power, but stable political systems normally also require legitimacy. Citizens are more likely to obey authority voluntarily when they regard it as lawful and justified.

These three concepts are fundamental to understanding political relationships.

Power: the ability to influence others' behaviour and outcomes, even against resistance (Weber, Dahl). It may be based on force, influence or authority, and may be political, economic or ideological. Lukes's three dimensions of power (decision-making, agenda-setting and preference-shaping) and Foucault's idea of diffused power show that power is found in all social relationships.

Authority: legitimate power that people accept as rightful. Weber's three types - traditional (custom and heredity), charismatic (personal qualities of a leader) and legal-rational (rules and procedures). Modern democracies rest mainly on legal-rational authority. Legitimacy: the belief that a government has the right to rule; it may come from tradition, charisma, legality, elections, ideology or performance. Without legitimacy, governments must rely on coercion, which is costly and unstable.

Relationship: power + legitimacy = authority. A government that has power but lacks legitimacy (such as a military regime) faces resistance; one with legitimacy obtains voluntary compliance. Democracies maintain legitimacy through elections, constitutional rule, protection of rights, accountability and good performance.

The state possesses population, territory, government and sovereignty. Government is the machinery that makes and implements public decisions on behalf of the state.

A nation is based on a shared sense of collective identity, while a nation-state broadly combines national identity with a political state. Citizenship defines formal membership in the state.

Citizenship carries both rights and responsibilities and connects the individual to political institutions.

State: a political community with population, territory, government and sovereignty. Theories of origin include divine right, force, social contract and evolutionary theories. Government: the machinery of the state with three organs - legislature, executive and judiciary; it is temporary, while the state is permanent.

Nation and nation-state: a nation is a community with a shared identity based on history, culture, language, religion or political will (Renan's 'daily plebiscite', Anderson's 'imagined community'). A nation-state combines a nation with a sovereign state; most states are multinational. Nationalism has been a powerful force for independence movements but can also lead to conflict.

Citizenship: membership of a state with rights and duties; acquired by birth, descent, registration or naturalisation; Marshall's three dimensions - civil, political and social rights. In India, the Constitution (Articles 5-11) and the Citizenship Act (1955) govern citizenship; India has single citizenship. Good citizenship requires awareness, participation, tolerance and performance of duties, such as the Fundamental Duties (Article 51A).

Liberty protects freedom, equality recognises equal worth, justice seeks fairness, and rights provide recognised claims and protections.

These ideas are closely connected. Rights help secure liberty; political equality supports democratic citizenship; justice concerns the fair arrangement of rights and opportunities.

Political debate often concerns how these values should be balanced in real institutions.

Liberty: negative and positive liberty; limited by law and the harm principle (Mill); civil, political, economic and national liberty; safeguards such as constitutional rights, independent judiciary and a free press. Equality: equal moral worth; legal, social, political and economic equality; equality of opportunity and affirmative action (reservations in India).

Justice: legal, social, economic and political justice; theories from Plato and Aristotle to Rawls's justice as fairness and Sen's comparative approach; the Indian Preamble's promise of social, economic and political justice. Rights: civil, political, economic and social rights; human rights (UDHR, 1948); the Fundamental Rights of the Indian Constitution, enforceable through courts (Article 32).

Interrelationship: rights give concrete form to liberty and equality; political equality supports democracy; justice harmonises liberty and equality by ensuring fair distribution of rights and opportunities. Debates continue over how to balance them - for example, freedom of speech versus protection from hate speech, or reservations (equality) versus merit and individual freedom.

Democracy is based on popular participation and consent. Rule of law and constitutional government help prevent arbitrary use of power.

Political parties organise electoral competition and seek to form governments. Pressure groups influence policy without normally seeking governmental office. Public opinion also affects political leaders and public decisions.

Together these institutions connect citizens with the political system.

Democracy: based on popular sovereignty and consent; direct and representative forms; parliamentary and presidential systems. Rule of law (Dicey's three principles; Article 14 in India) and constitutionalism prevent arbitrary power. The constitution establishes institutions, distributes powers and protects rights.

Political parties contest elections, form governments or opposition, aggregate interests, make policies and recruit leaders; party systems may be one-party, two-party or multi-party. Pressure groups (business, labour, farmers, professional, issue-based) influence policies through lobbying, campaigns, protests and litigation without seeking office. Public opinion, formed by media, parties, groups, education and social media, guides and controls government.

Together, these institutions link citizens with the state: parties provide choices, pressure groups represent specific interests, public opinion provides feedback, and constitutional rules ensure that power is exercised within limits. A healthy democracy needs strong, internally democratic parties, a free press, active civil society and informed citizens.
The Constitution was framed by the Constituent Assembly after extensive debate about democracy, rights, federalism and social transformation.

The Constituent Assembly was formed under the Cabinet Mission Plan (1946), with members indirectly elected by provincial assemblies (292) and nominated by princely states (93), plus 4 from Chief Commissioners' provinces - 389 in total, reduced to 299 after Partition. It first met on 9 December 1946 with Dr Sachchidananda Sinha as temporary chairman; Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President (11 December 1946), and B. N. Rau was the constitutional adviser. Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946, adopted on 22 January 1947, which became the basis of the Preamble.

Important committees included the Drafting Committee (chaired by Dr B. R. Ambedkar, set up on 29 August 1947), the Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees (Nehru), the Provincial Constitution Committee and the Advisory Committee on Fundamental Rights, Minorities and Tribal and Excluded Areas (Sardar Patel). The Assembly took 2 years, 11 months and 18 days, holding 11 sessions. The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day), the anniversary of the Purna Swaraj declaration of 1930.
The Preamble expresses the basic ideals of the Constitution and describes India as a sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic committed to justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

The Preamble reads: 'We, the people of India, having solemnly resolved to constitute India into a Sovereign Socialist Secular Democratic Republic and to secure to all its citizens: Justice, social, economic and political; Liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship; Equality of status and of opportunity; and to promote among them all Fraternity assuring the dignity of the individual and the unity and integrity of the Nation; in our Constituent Assembly this twenty-sixth day of November, 1949, do hereby adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution.'

The words 'Socialist', 'Secular' and 'integrity' were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976). The Preamble shows that the source of authority is the people. In the Berubari case (1960), the Supreme Court said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution, but in Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) it held that the Preamble is part of the Constitution and can be amended, though not in a way that destroys the basic structure. K. M. Munshi called it the 'political horoscope' of the Constitution, and Ernest Barker called it the 'key-note'.
Fundamental Rights protect important freedoms and legal guarantees against arbitrary state action.

Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12-35), called the 'Magna Carta of India'. Originally seven, there are now six: (1) Right to Equality (Articles 14-18); (2) Right to Freedom (Articles 19-22), including six freedoms under Article 19 - speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence and profession - and protection of life and personal liberty (Article 21); (3) Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24); (4) Right to Freedom of Religion (Articles 25-28); (5) Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29-30); and (6) Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32). The Right to Property (Article 31) was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978).

Features: they are justiciable (enforceable through courts), not absolute (subject to reasonable restrictions), some are available only to citizens (Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30) and others to all persons, and they can be suspended during a national emergency (except Articles 20 and 21, after the 44th Amendment). The Supreme Court has expanded Article 21 to include rights such as livelihood, privacy (K. S. Puttaswamy, 2017), clean environment, education, shelter and speedy trial (Maneka Gandhi case, 1978, introduced 'due process' reasoning).
Directive Principles guide the state in promoting social and economic welfare, although they are not enforceable by courts in the same way as Fundamental Rights.

Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) are in Part IV (Articles 36-51), borrowed from the Irish Constitution. Article 37 says they are not enforceable by any court but are 'fundamental in the governance of the country', and it is the duty of the state to apply them in making laws. Ambedkar called them 'novel features' of the Constitution; Granville Austin described them, with Fundamental Rights, as the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

They can be classified as: socialist principles (Article 38 - social order based on justice; Article 39 - adequate livelihood, equitable distribution of resources, equal pay for equal work; Article 41 - right to work, education and public assistance; Article 42 - humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Article 43 - living wage); Gandhian principles (Article 40 - village panchayats; Article 43 - cottage industries; Article 46 - promotion of interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections; Article 47 - prohibition of intoxicating drinks; Article 48 - prohibition of cow slaughter); and liberal-intellectual principles (Article 44 - uniform civil code; Article 45 - early childhood care; Article 48A - environment; Article 50 - separation of judiciary from executive; Article 51 - international peace). In Minerva Mills (1980), the Supreme Court held that harmony and balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP is part of the basic structure.
Fundamental Duties state civic responsibilities expected from citizens.

Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the recommendation of the Swaran Singh Committee, as Part IVA, Article 51A, inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR. Originally ten, an eleventh was added by the 86th Amendment (2002). They include: to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals, the National Flag and the National Anthem; to cherish the ideals of the freedom struggle; to uphold the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; to defend the country; to promote harmony and renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women; to preserve the composite culture; to protect the environment; to develop scientific temper and the spirit of inquiry; to safeguard public property and abjure violence; to strive for excellence; and for parents or guardians to provide educational opportunities to children aged 6 to 14.

They are not directly enforceable by courts but can be enforced through laws (such as the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971) and help courts interpret laws. They remind citizens that rights and duties go together. The Verma Committee (1999) suggested ways to make them operational.
The President is the constitutional head of the Union and normally exercises executive functions on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers.

The President (Articles 52-62) is elected indirectly by an electoral college of the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of the state legislative assemblies (including Delhi and Puducherry), by proportional representation through the single transferable vote and secret ballot (Article 55 ensures parity between the Union and the states). The term is five years; the President can be re-elected. Qualifications: a citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha and not holding an office of profit. The President can be removed by impeachment for violation of the Constitution (Article 61).

Powers: executive (appointment of the Prime Minister, ministers, Governors, judges, the CAG, Election Commissioners), legislative (summoning and proroguing Parliament, dissolving the Lok Sabha, assent to bills, ordinances under Article 123), financial (money bills require recommendation), judicial (pardon under Article 72), military (Supreme Commander) and emergency powers (Articles 352, 356, 360). The 42nd (1976) and 44th (1978) Amendments made the advice of the Council of Ministers binding, though the President may return it once for reconsideration (Article 74). Discretion exists in situations such as a hung Parliament and the 'pocket veto'. Droupadi Murmu became the 15th President in 2022.
The Prime Minister is the head of government and the central political executive in the parliamentary system.

The Prime Minister is appointed by the President (Article 75); by convention, the President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition in the Lok Sabha. The PM must be a member of Parliament or become one within six months. The PM's term is not fixed; they hold office as long as they enjoy the confidence of the Lok Sabha.

Powers and functions: forms the Council of Ministers and allocates portfolios; presides over Cabinet meetings; coordinates government policies; is the chief link between the President and the Council of Ministers (Article 78); is the leader of the Lok Sabha (if a member); advises the President on dissolving the Lok Sabha; chairs NITI Aayog, the National Development Council and other bodies; and represents India internationally. The PM is described as 'first among equals' (primus inter pares), but in practice is the keystone of the cabinet arch; the position's strength depends on party majority and personality (Nehru, Indira Gandhi, Narendra Modi with strong majorities; coalition PMs with weaker positions).
The Council of Ministers assists and advises the President and is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

The Council of Ministers (Article 74 and 75) includes three categories: Cabinet Ministers (senior ministers heading major departments), Ministers of State (with independent charge or assisting Cabinet ministers) and Deputy Ministers. The Cabinet is the smaller, more powerful core that makes major decisions. The 91st Amendment (2003) limited the size of the Council of Ministers to 15 percent of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.

Principles of working: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)) - the ministry stands or falls together, and a vote of no confidence forces its resignation; individual responsibility to the President (ministers hold office during the President's pleasure, on the PM's advice); and the secrecy of cabinet proceedings (oath of secrecy). The Council of Ministers exercises the real executive power in India's parliamentary system.
Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha and performs legislative, financial, deliberative and accountability functions.

Parliament (Articles 79-122) consists of the President, the Lok Sabha (House of the People) and the Rajya Sabha (Council of States). It is a bicameral legislature. Functions: legislative (making laws on Union and Concurrent List subjects, and on State List subjects in certain circumstances); financial (passing the budget, approving taxes and expenditure); control over the executive (question hour, zero hour, adjournment motions, calling attention motions, no-confidence motions, parliamentary committees such as the Public Accounts Committee); constituent (amending the Constitution under Article 368); electoral (electing the President and Vice-President); and judicial (impeachment of the President, removal of judges).

Sessions: the President summons Parliament at least twice a year with a gap of not more than six months; normally there are three sessions (Budget, Monsoon and Winter). Joint sittings (Article 108) are held to resolve deadlocks on ordinary bills; they have occurred three times (1961, 1978, 2002). A new Parliament building was inaugurated in 2023.
The Lok Sabha is the directly elected House of the People and is central to government formation and financial control.

The Lok Sabha has a maximum strength of 552 under the Constitution (currently 543 elected members; the two nominated Anglo-Indian seats were abolished by the 104th Amendment, 2019). Members are directly elected from territorial constituencies by universal adult franchise for five years, unless dissolved earlier. Seats are reserved for SCs (84) and STs (47); the Women's Reservation Act (106th Amendment, 2023) provides for one-third reservation for women after the next census and delimitation. Qualifications: citizen, at least 25 years old. The Speaker presides; the first Speaker was G. V. Mavalankar.

Special powers of the Lok Sabha: money bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha (Article 110), and the Rajya Sabha can only delay them for 14 days; the Speaker certifies whether a bill is a money bill; the Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha, which alone can pass a no-confidence motion; and in a joint sitting the Lok Sabha's larger numbers usually prevail. Mizoram elects one member to the Lok Sabha.
The Rajya Sabha represents the states at the Union level and is a permanent chamber.

The Rajya Sabha has a maximum strength of 250 - 238 representatives of states and Union Territories elected by elected members of state assemblies through proportional representation by single transferable vote, and 12 members nominated by the President for expertise in literature, science, art and social service. At present it has 245 members. It is a permanent House that cannot be dissolved; one-third of members retire every two years, and members serve six-year terms. The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman.

Seats are allotted to states according to population (Fourth Schedule): Uttar Pradesh has 31, while Mizoram and other small states have one each. Special powers: under Article 249, it can authorise Parliament to make laws on a State List subject in the national interest by a two-thirds majority; under Article 312, it can authorise the creation of new All-India Services. It acts as a revising chamber, represents the federal principle and provides a place for experienced people. Critics point to its weaker powers on money bills and the election of members from outside the states they represent.
The Supreme Court is the highest court and protects the Constitution through judicial review and constitutional interpretation.

The Supreme Court (Articles 124-147) was established on 28 January 1950. It consists of the Chief Justice of India and other judges (originally 7, now a maximum of 33 plus the CJI, total 34, since 2019). Judges are appointed by the President after consultation; the 'collegium system' (developed by the Second Judges Case, 1993, and Third Judges Case, 1998) gives a collegium of the CJI and four senior judges the decisive role. The National Judicial Appointments Commission Act (99th Amendment, 2014) was struck down in 2015. Judges retire at 65 and can be removed only by Parliament through a special majority on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

Jurisdiction: original (disputes between the Union and states, Article 131), writ jurisdiction (Article 32 - enforcement of Fundamental Rights through habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto), appellate (constitutional, civil and criminal appeals, special leave petitions under Article 136), advisory (Article 143), and as a court of record (Article 129, power to punish for contempt). It is the guardian of the Constitution and protector of Fundamental Rights. Public Interest Litigation (PIL), introduced in the late 1970s and 1980s by Justices P. N. Bhagwati and V. R. Krishna Iyer, expanded access to justice.
Judicial review is the power of courts to examine whether laws and government actions are consistent with the Constitution.

Judicial review originated in the USA in Marbury v. Madison (1803), when Chief Justice John Marshall declared that courts could strike down laws contrary to the Constitution. In India, it is based on Articles 13 (laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void), 32, 226 (High Courts' writ jurisdiction) and 368. Courts can review legislative acts, executive actions and even constitutional amendments.

Important cases: Shankari Prasad (1951) and Sajjan Singh (1965) allowed amendment of Fundamental Rights; Golak Nath (1967) said Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; Kesavananda Bharati (1973) established the 'basic structure doctrine' - Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot destroy its basic structure (including supremacy of the Constitution, democracy, secularism, federalism, separation of powers, judicial review and the rule of law); Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975), Minerva Mills (1980) and S. R. Bommai (1994) reinforced it. The Ninth Schedule laws were made subject to review in I. R. Coelho (2007). Judicial review is itself part of the basic structure. Critics warn of 'judicial overreach' and 'judicial activism', while supporters say it protects rights and constitutional values.
Indian federalism divides powers between the Union and states while giving the Union significant authority in several areas.

The Constitution describes India as a 'Union of States' (Article 1), not a federation. Federal features: a written and rigid constitution, division of powers through three lists in the Seventh Schedule (Union List - originally 97 subjects, now 98; State List - originally 66, now 59; Concurrent List - originally 47, now 52), an independent judiciary to settle disputes, a bicameral legislature with the Rajya Sabha representing states, and supremacy of the Constitution.

Unitary features: a strong Centre, residuary powers with the Union (Article 248), single citizenship, single constitution (except Jammu and Kashmir until 2019), integrated judiciary, All-India Services, appointment of Governors by the Centre, emergency provisions, Parliament's power to change state boundaries (Article 3), and the Centre's power to legislate on state subjects in certain conditions (Articles 249, 250, 252, 253). K. C. Wheare called India 'quasi-federal'; Ivor Jennings called it 'a federation with a strong centralising tendency'; Granville Austin called it 'cooperative federalism'; and the Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai (1994) declared federalism a basic feature. Recent terms include 'competitive federalism' and 'cooperative federalism' (NITI Aayog, GST Council).
Centre-State relations include legislative, administrative and financial relations between the Union and state governments.

Legislative relations (Articles 245-255): Parliament can make laws for the whole or any part of India; states for their own territory. Subjects are divided into the three lists. Parliament can legislate on State List subjects when the Rajya Sabha passes a resolution (Article 249), during an emergency (Article 250), when two or more states request (Article 252), to implement international treaties (Article 253), and under President's Rule. In conflicts on Concurrent subjects, Union law prevails (Article 254). Governors can reserve state bills for the President's consideration (Article 200-201).

Administrative relations (Articles 256-263): states must comply with Union laws; the Centre can give directions to states; All-India Services; the Inter-State Council (Article 263, set up in 1990); Governors as agents of the Centre; and Article 356 (President's Rule), used over 100 times, often misused before the Bommai judgement (1994). Financial relations (Articles 264-293): division of taxing powers; the Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends sharing of central taxes and grants; the GST (101st Amendment, 2016) created the GST Council. Commissions on Centre-State relations include the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966), the Rajamannar Committee (Tamil Nadu, 1969), the Sarkaria Commission (1983-1988) and the Punchhi Commission (2007-2010). Issues include the misuse of Article 356, the role of Governors, financial dependence and demands for greater autonomy.
The Election Commission supervises and conducts elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President.

The Election Commission of India (Article 324), established on 25 January 1950 (National Voters' Day), superintends, directs and controls the preparation of electoral rolls and the conduct of elections to Parliament, state legislatures and the offices of President and Vice-President. Since 1993, it has been a three-member body consisting of a Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners. The CEC can be removed only like a Supreme Court judge. Sukumar Sen was the first CEC. T. N. Seshan (1990-1996) strictly enforced the Model Code of Conduct.

Functions: delimitation-related work, preparation and revision of electoral rolls, issuing voter ID cards (EPIC), recognising political parties and allotting symbols, scheduling elections, enforcing the Model Code of Conduct, supervising election expenditure, deciding disputes on symbols, and conducting elections using Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs, used nationwide since 2004) and VVPAT. Issues include money power, criminalisation, paid news, misuse of social media and debates about the appointment process (the 2023 Act on appointment of Election Commissioners). State Election Commissions (Articles 243K and 243ZA) conduct local body elections.
Political parties organise elections, represent interests and form governments. India has national and regional parties.

The Election Commission recognises parties as national or state parties based on criteria such as the percentage of votes and seats won in Lok Sabha or Assembly elections (a national party must, for example, win at least 6 percent of votes in four or more states and four Lok Sabha seats, or 2 percent of Lok Sabha seats from at least three states, or be a recognised state party in four states). As of 2023, there are six national parties: the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), the Indian National Congress (INC), the Communist Party of India (Marxist), the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP), the Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) and the National People's Party (NPP) of Meghalaya.

The party system has evolved through phases: one-party dominance of the Congress ('Congress system', Rajni Kothari, 1952-1967); the decline of Congress and the rise of opposition and regional parties (1967-1989, with the Janata government of 1977); the era of coalitions (1989-2014 - National Front, United Front, NDA, UPA); and BJP dominance since 2014. Regional parties include the DMK, AIADMK, TMC, Shiv Sena, TDP, BJD, SP, RJD, JD(U) and MNF and ZPM in Mizoram. Issues include lack of internal democracy, dynastic politics, defections and funding (the electoral bond scheme was struck down by the Supreme Court in 2024).
Caste influences political mobilisation, representation and electoral behaviour, while democratic politics can also reshape caste relations.

Rajni Kothari ('Caste in Indian Politics', 1970) argued that caste has been 'politicised' and politics 'casteised': caste groups are mobilised for votes, parties select candidates according to the caste composition of constituencies, and caste associations act as pressure groups. Lloyd and Susanne Rudolph described the 'modernity of tradition', in which caste associations became vehicles of democratic participation.

Caste-based mobilisation includes the rise of OBC politics after the Mandal Commission (1980, implemented 1990, with 27 percent reservation for OBCs), Dalit parties such as the BSP (Kanshi Ram, Mayawati), parties based on caste coalitions (the SP, RJD), and caste census debates (Bihar's caste survey of 2023). Reservations in legislatures, jobs and education for SCs and STs (Articles 15(4), 16(4), 330, 332) have increased representation. Effects: positive (empowerment of marginalised groups, wider participation) and negative (vote-bank politics, conflicts between castes, neglect of merit and development issues).
Religion influences political identities and debates, but the constitutional order is committed to secular government.

Indian secularism, as described in the Constitution (Articles 25-28 and the Preamble), means that the state has no official religion, treats all religions equally (sarva dharma sambhava), guarantees freedom of religion to all and does not discriminate on religious grounds. Unlike the Western model of strict separation of church and state, Indian secularism allows state intervention in religious matters for social reform (for example, temple entry laws, abolition of untouchability and regulation of religious institutions) - Rajeev Bhargava calls it 'principled distance'.

Religion has influenced politics through communal parties, riots (Partition, 1984 anti-Sikh riots, Babri Masjid demolition 1992, Gujarat 2002), debates on the Uniform Civil Code, the Shah Bano case (1985), the Ram Janmabhoomi movement and the Supreme Court's Ayodhya judgement (2019), the Citizenship Amendment Act (2019) and the rise of Hindutva politics. Critics argue that some parties practise 'vote-bank' politics or majoritarianism. The Supreme Court in S. R. Bommai (1994) held secularism to be part of the basic structure.
Regionalism refers to political mobilisation based on regional identity, interests or demands for autonomy.

Regionalism is loyalty to a particular region and the demand for its interests, identity and autonomy. Causes include linguistic and cultural identity, uneven economic development, historical factors, geographical isolation, the neglect of regions by the Centre, sons-of-the-soil feelings and the role of regional parties. Forms include demands for separate states (Telangana, created in 2014; Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Uttarakhand, created in 2000), greater autonomy (Tamil Nadu's DMK, Punjab's Anandpur Sahib Resolution, 1973), inter-state disputes (water - Kaveri; boundaries - Assam-Mizoram), and secessionism (insurgencies in the Northeast, Khalistan, Kashmir).

The States Reorganisation Commission (Fazl Ali, 1953-1955) led to the reorganisation of states on linguistic lines (1956), after the death of Potti Sriramulu fasting for Andhra (1952). Regionalism can be positive - promoting regional development, culture and federal balance - or negative, threatening national unity when it becomes separatist or chauvinistic (anti-migrant movements). Responses include federalism, special provisions (Articles 371-371J), autonomous councils and balanced development.
Coalition government occurs when multiple parties cooperate to form a government because no single party has sufficient support.

A coalition government is formed when two or more parties combine because no single party has a majority. Coalitions may be pre-poll (alliances before elections) or post-poll. In India, coalition politics began at the state level in 1967 (the Samyukta Vidhayak Dal governments) and at the Centre with the Janata Party government (1977-1979). From 1989 to 2014, no single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha: the National Front (V. P. Singh, 1989), the United Front (1996-1998), the NDA under Atal Bihari Vajpayee (1998-2004) and the UPA under Manmohan Singh (2004-2014) were coalitions.

Advantages: wider representation of regional and social groups, consensus-based decision-making and checks on the dominance of one party. Disadvantages: instability (governments falling due to withdrawal of support), policy paralysis, bargaining and 'coalition dharma' compromises, and disproportionate influence of small parties. Coalitions use mechanisms such as a Common Minimum Programme and coordination committees. Even after 2014, the BJP governs with NDA allies, and after the 2024 elections, the BJP needed allies (TDP, JD(U)) to form a majority.

The Constitution was framed by the Constituent Assembly and established India as a democratic republic. The Preamble expresses the central constitutional ideals of justice, liberty, equality and fraternity.

Fundamental Rights protect individual freedoms and legal equality. Directive Principles guide the state toward social and economic welfare, while Fundamental Duties identify civic responsibilities.

Together these provisions combine political democracy with the constitutional goal of social transformation.

Making of the Constitution: the Constituent Assembly (1946-1949), with Rajendra Prasad as President and Ambedkar as Chairman of the Drafting Committee; the Objectives Resolution (1946); adoption on 26 November 1949; commencement on 26 January 1950. Sources: the Government of India Act 1935 (federal scheme, emergency provisions, Governor's office), British Constitution (parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship), US Constitution (Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary, impeachment), Irish Constitution (DPSP, nomination to Rajya Sabha), Canada (strong Centre), Australia (Concurrent List), Weimar Germany (suspension of rights in emergency), USSR (Fundamental Duties) and France (republic, liberty, equality, fraternity).

Salient features: lengthiest written constitution; blend of rigidity and flexibility; parliamentary form of government; federal system with unitary bias; Fundamental Rights, DPSP and Fundamental Duties; independent and integrated judiciary; universal adult franchise; secular state; single citizenship; emergency provisions; independent bodies (Election Commission, CAG, UPSC); three-tier government (panchayats and municipalities after 1992); and special provisions for SCs, STs and certain states.

Preamble: sovereign, socialist, secular, democratic republic; justice, liberty, equality and fraternity. Rights, DPSP and Duties together express political democracy (rights), social and economic democracy (DPSP) and civic responsibility (duties). The Constitution is a 'living document' that has been amended over 100 times, guided by the basic structure doctrine.

India follows a parliamentary system. The President is the constitutional head, while effective political leadership is exercised by the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Parliament consists of the President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha and makes laws, approves finances, debates public issues and holds the executive accountable.

The relationship between executive and legislature is therefore central to Indian parliamentary government.

President: the constitutional head, elected indirectly for five years; executive, legislative, financial, judicial, military and emergency powers; acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74), with limited discretion (appointment of the PM in a hung Parliament, returning advice once, pocket veto). The Vice-President is the ex officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha and acts as President when needed.

Prime Minister and Council of Ministers: the real executive; the PM is appointed by the President as leader of the majority in the Lok Sabha, forms the ministry, presides over the Cabinet, coordinates policy and leads the nation; the Council of Ministers (limited to 15 percent of Lok Sabha strength) is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha. Parliament: the President, Lok Sabha (543 elected, five-year term, directly elected, controls money bills and confidence) and Rajya Sabha (245, permanent house, represents states).

Executive-legislature relations: the executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature; Parliament controls the executive through questions, debates, motions, committees and financial control; the executive leads the legislature through party majority and initiative in legislation. With strong majorities, the executive dominates ('cabinet dictatorship'); with coalitions, Parliament is more influential. Declining sittings, disruptions and frequent use of ordinances are concerns about the functioning of Parliament.

The Supreme Court is the highest judicial institution in India. It interprets the Constitution, decides constitutional disputes and protects Fundamental Rights.

Judicial review allows courts to test laws and executive actions against constitutional requirements. This power helps maintain constitutional supremacy and limits arbitrary government.

The judiciary therefore plays a central role in India's constitutional system.

Organisation: the Chief Justice of India and up to 33 other judges; appointed by the President through the collegium system; retirement at 65; removal only by Parliament through a special majority. Independence is secured by security of tenure, fixed salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, prohibition of practice after retirement, power to punish for contempt, and separation from the executive (Article 50).

Jurisdiction: original, writ (Article 32 - Ambedkar called it 'the heart and soul of the Constitution'), appellate, advisory (Article 143) and court of record (Article 129). Judicial review allows the Court to declare laws and executive actions unconstitutional; the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973) limits Parliament's amending power. Judicial activism through PIL has addressed issues such as bonded labour, prisoners' rights, environment (M. C. Mehta cases), sexual harassment (Vishaka, 1997) and the right to food.

Evaluation: the Supreme Court has protected Fundamental Rights, upheld federalism (Bommai), secularism and the rule of law, and expanded Article 21. Criticisms include pendency of cases (over 80,000 in the Supreme Court and millions in lower courts), the opacity of the collegium system, judicial overreach into policy matters and delays. The judiciary is nevertheless central to maintaining constitutional supremacy and limiting arbitrary government.

India divides legislative and administrative authority between the Union and states. The Constitution creates federal institutions but also gives the Union strong powers in important areas.

Centre-State relations involve legislative, administrative and financial dimensions. Political developments, regional parties and demands for autonomy have also shaped federal practice.

Indian federalism is therefore both constitutional and political in character.

Nature of Indian federalism: federal features (written constitution, division of powers, independent judiciary, bicameralism) combined with unitary features (strong Centre, residuary powers, single citizenship, All-India Services, Governors, emergency powers, Parliament's power to reorganise states). Scholars describe it as quasi-federal (Wheare), cooperative (Austin), bargaining federalism (Morris-Jones) or asymmetrical federalism (special provisions for certain states under Articles 371A-371J, Sixth Schedule areas).

Centre-State relations: legislative (three lists and Union supremacy in conflicts), administrative (directions to states, Governors, All-India Services, Article 356) and financial (division of taxes, Finance Commission, grants, GST Council). Tensions have arisen over the misuse of Article 356 (before Bommai, 1994), the role and appointment of Governors, delays in assent to state bills (the Supreme Court in 2023-2024 set limits on such delays), financial dependence, central agencies and the control of police and resources.

Political factors: the dominance of the Congress until 1967 kept tensions low; the rise of regional parties and coalitions increased states' bargaining power; and since 2014 strong central governments have again centralised power, while also promoting 'cooperative federalism' (NITI Aayog replacing the Planning Commission, 2015; GST). Commissions (Sarkaria, Punchhi) recommended greater consultation and restraint in using Article 356. Indian federalism is thus shaped by both the Constitution and political practice.

sections.title: Political Processes and Issues in India

blocks.text:
Political parties connect citizens with government and organise electoral competition. The Election Commission plays a key role in conducting elections.

Caste, religion and regional identity influence political mobilisation. Regional parties and coalition governments have become important features of Indian politics.

These factors demonstrate that Indian democracy operates through both constitutional institutions and complex social forces.

Political parties and elections: India has a multi-party system with national and regional parties; the party system has evolved from Congress dominance to coalitions to BJP dominance. Elections are conducted by the Election Commission through universal adult franchise, the first-past-the-post system and EVMs. Indian elections are the largest in the world (about 97 crore voters in 2024). Problems include money power, criminalisation, defections, misuse of government machinery and fake news; reforms include the Model Code of Conduct, expenditure limits, NOTA (2013), disclosure of criminal records and the anti-defection law.

Social factors: caste is mobilised in elections and through reservations; religion shapes identity politics and debates on secularism; regionalism leads to demands for states, autonomy and regional parties; language, tribe and class also influence politics. Coalition politics (1989-2014) gave regional parties an important role at the Centre.

Evaluation: Indian democracy has deepened through high voter turnout (especially among women and the poor), peaceful transfers of power and the rise of marginalised groups (Yogendra Yadav's 'second democratic upsurge'). At the same time, challenges remain: communal polarisation, caste conflict, criminalisation, the weakening of institutions and inequality. Indian democracy thus works through both constitutional institutions and complex social forces.
Comparative politics studies and compares political institutions and processes across different countries.

Comparative politics studies political systems, institutions and processes across countries to find similarities, differences and general patterns. Aristotle compared 158 Greek constitutions; Montesquieu, Tocqueville ('Democracy in America', 1835-1840) and Bryce ('Modern Democracies', 1921) continued the tradition. The traditional approach focused on formal institutions and constitutions, mainly of Western countries.

After the Second World War, the modern approach (Gabriel Almond, Sidney Verba, David Easton, Lucian Pye) broadened the scope to include developing countries, political culture ('The Civic Culture', Almond and Verba, 1963), political development, political socialisation and behaviour, using methods such as systems analysis and structural-functionalism. Comparative politics helps us understand why democracies succeed or fail, the effects of electoral systems and federalism, and lessons from other countries' experiences. Methods include case studies, comparisons of few cases and statistical comparisons of many countries.
A political system includes institutions and processes through which authoritative decisions are made in a society.

David Easton ('The Political System', 1953; 'A Systems Analysis of Political Life', 1965) defined the political system as the set of interactions through which values are authoritatively allocated for a society. It receives inputs (demands and supports) from the environment, converts them through institutions into outputs (decisions and policies), which produce feedback that affects new inputs. The system tries to maintain itself in a changing environment.

Gabriel Almond's structural-functional approach identified input functions (political socialisation and recruitment, interest articulation, interest aggregation, political communication) and output functions (rule-making, rule application and rule adjudication), performed by structures such as parties, pressure groups, legislatures, executives and courts. The political system is broader than the state, including informal institutions and behaviour. Critics argue that systems analysis is too abstract and conservative, emphasising stability over change.
In a parliamentary system, the executive emerges from the legislature and remains politically responsible to it.

The parliamentary system originated in Britain and is also called cabinet or responsible government. Features: a nominal or titular head of state (monarch or president) and a real executive (the Prime Minister and Cabinet); the executive is drawn from the legislature; collective responsibility of the cabinet to the lower house; the government can be removed by a vote of no confidence; the leadership of the Prime Minister; dissolution of the lower house before its term; and fusion of powers between executive and legislature. Countries include Britain, India, Canada, Australia, Japan and Germany.

Merits: harmony between executive and legislature, responsible government, flexibility (governments can be changed without waiting for elections), and representation of diverse groups in the cabinet. Demerits: instability in coalitions or with weak majorities, cabinet dictatorship with strong majorities, violation of the separation of powers and a temptation to place party interests over national interest. Walter Bagehot ('The English Constitution', 1867) described the cabinet as 'a hyphen which joins, a buckle which fastens, the legislative part of the state to the executive part'.
In a presidential system, the president normally has a fixed tenure and is institutionally separate from the legislature.

The presidential system is best illustrated by the USA. Features: the President is both head of state and head of government; elected (directly or through an electoral college) for a fixed term (four years in the USA, maximum two terms by the 22nd Amendment, 1951); the President and cabinet secretaries are not members of the legislature; the President is not responsible to the legislature and cannot be removed by a no-confidence vote (only by impeachment); the legislature cannot be dissolved by the President; and there is separation of powers with checks and balances. Other examples include Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia and the Philippines; France and Russia have semi-presidential systems.

Merits: stability (fixed terms), strong leadership, separation of powers that protects liberty, and the ability to appoint experts to the cabinet. Demerits: possibility of deadlock between the executive and legislature (especially in 'divided government', when different parties control the presidency and Congress), rigidity (difficult to remove an incompetent president), and danger of authoritarianism in some countries. Juan Linz ('The Perils of Presidentialism', 1990) argued that parliamentary systems are more stable for new democracies.
The British Constitution is based on statutes, conventions, judicial decisions and historical practices rather than one single codified constitutional document.

Britain has no single written constitution. Its sources include: historical charters and statutes (Magna Carta 1215, the Petition of Right 1628, the Bill of Rights 1689, the Act of Settlement 1701, the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949, the Human Rights Act 1998, the Constitutional Reform Act 2005, the Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland devolution acts of 1998), judicial decisions (common law), conventions, and works of authority (Dicey, Bagehot, Erskine May). The UK's membership of the European Union (1973-2020) also affected its constitution until Brexit.

Features: unwritten (uncodified) and flexible - any law can be changed by an ordinary Act of Parliament; parliamentary sovereignty - Parliament can make or unmake any law, and no court can strike down an Act of Parliament; constitutional monarchy - the monarch reigns but does not rule; unitary state with devolution; rule of law; parliamentary government; bicameral Parliament; and an independent judiciary (the Supreme Court of the UK was created in 2009, replacing the Law Lords of the House of Lords). Britain is called the 'mother of parliaments'.
Rule of law means that public authority is exercised according to law and that legal rules apply to rulers as well as citizens.

A. V. Dicey explained the rule of law as a key feature of the British constitution: (1) absence of arbitrary power - no one can be punished except for a breach of law proved before ordinary courts; (2) equality before the law - every person, whatever their rank, is subject to the ordinary law and the jurisdiction of ordinary courts; there is no separate administrative law for officials (as in France's 'droit administratif'); (3) the general principles of the constitution, such as personal liberty and freedom of assembly, are the result of judicial decisions in particular cases, rather than being derived from a written constitution.

Criticism: Dicey's description was not fully accurate even in his time, since officials enjoyed special powers and immunities, and the growth of the welfare state led to delegated legislation and administrative tribunals. Lord Bingham ('The Rule of Law', 2010) offered a broader modern definition, including accessibility of law, equality, human rights, fair trial and compliance with international law. The rule of law remains a core principle of British and Indian constitutional government.
Conventions are non-legal but accepted rules that guide the working of the British constitutional system.

Conventions are unwritten rules of political behaviour that are generally followed, though they are not enforced by courts. Dicey called them 'rules for determining the mode in which the discretionary powers of the Crown ought to be exercised'. Examples: the monarch gives royal assent to bills passed by Parliament (the last refusal was in 1708 by Queen Anne); the monarch appoints the leader of the majority party in the House of Commons as Prime Minister; the Prime Minister must be a member of the House of Commons; the cabinet is collectively responsible to the Commons; a government defeated on a vote of confidence must resign or call an election; the monarch acts on the advice of ministers; and the House of Lords does not reject the government's manifesto bills (the Salisbury Convention).

Conventions are obeyed because breaking them would cause political crisis, public criticism or legal changes, and because they reflect democratic principles. They make the British constitution flexible. India has also adopted many conventions, such as appointing the leader of the majority party as Prime Minister.
The British Parliament consists of the Crown, House of Lords and House of Commons.

The British Parliament, at Westminster, consists of the Crown (the monarch, currently King Charles III since 2022), the House of Lords (upper house) and the House of Commons (lower house). Legislation requires the approval of both houses and the royal assent (except under the Parliament Acts). Parliament is sovereign: it can make or repeal any law; no Parliament can bind its successors; and no court can declare an Act invalid.

Functions: making laws; controlling finance (budget and taxes); scrutinising the government through Question Time (including Prime Minister's Questions), debates, select committees and no-confidence motions; representing the people; and making and breaking governments. The Speaker of the House of Commons is impartial and leaves their party on election; by convention, the Speaker is re-elected unopposed by major parties.
The House of Commons is the elected chamber and is the dominant legislative house in modern British politics.

The House of Commons has 650 members (MPs) elected from single-member constituencies by the first-past-the-post system, for a maximum term of five years (the Fixed-term Parliaments Act 2011 was repealed in 2022, restoring the Prime Minister's power to request dissolution). The government is formed by the party commanding a majority; the second-largest party forms 'His Majesty's Most Loyal Opposition', with a 'shadow cabinet'.

The Commons is the dominant house: money bills must originate there and the Lords cannot delay them for more than one month (Parliament Act 1911); the Lords can delay other bills for only one year (Parliament Act 1949); the government is responsible to the Commons, which can force its resignation through a vote of no confidence (as in 1979, when James Callaghan's government lost by one vote). The Commons is thus the centre of British democracy.
The House of Lords is the upper chamber and performs legislative revision, debate and scrutiny functions.

The House of Lords is not elected. Its members include life peers (appointed by the monarch on the advice of the Prime Minister, under the Life Peerages Act 1958 - the majority), 92 hereditary peers (after the House of Lords Act 1999 removed most hereditary peers), and 26 Lords Spiritual (bishops of the Church of England). Its size is around 800, making it one of the largest legislative chambers. Until 2009, the Law Lords served as the highest court of appeal; this role was transferred to the Supreme Court.

Functions: revising and scrutinising legislation, proposing amendments, delaying bills (up to one year), debating issues, and scrutinising government through committees with expert members. Its powers are limited by the Parliament Acts of 1911 and 1949 and the Salisbury Convention. Debate continues on reform - whether it should be elected, reduced in size or abolished - because an unelected chamber seems undemocratic, though supporters value the expertise and independence of its members.
The Prime Minister leads the government and normally commands the confidence of the House of Commons.

The office developed in the eighteenth century, with Sir Robert Walpole (1721-1742) regarded as the first Prime Minister. The monarch appoints the leader of the majority party in the House of Commons, by convention, and the PM must be a member of the Commons. The PM's official residence is 10 Downing Street.

Powers: selects and dismisses ministers; chairs the Cabinet; controls the agenda and Cabinet committees; leads the majority party; advises the monarch on appointments (peers, bishops, senior officials) and dissolution; leads foreign and defence policy; and represents Britain abroad. Descriptions range from 'first among equals' to 'elected monarch' and 'prime ministerial government' (Richard Crossman). The PM's power depends on the party's majority and popularity - strong PMs such as Margaret Thatcher and Tony Blair, while others (Theresa May, Liz Truss, who served only 49 days in 2022) were weakened by party divisions. Keir Starmer became Prime Minister after the Labour victory in July 2024.
The Cabinet is the senior group of ministers responsible for major government policy and collective political leadership.

The Cabinet consists of about 20-25 senior ministers chosen by the Prime Minister from the majority party, usually from the House of Commons, with a few from the Lords. Key members include the Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance), the Foreign Secretary and the Home Secretary. The Cabinet determines government policy, controls the executive departments, initiates legislation and coordinates administration. It works through Cabinet committees and the Cabinet Office.

Principles: collective responsibility (ministers must publicly support Cabinet decisions or resign), individual ministerial responsibility for their departments, confidentiality of proceedings, and the leadership of the PM. Bagehot called the Cabinet the 'efficient secret' of the English constitution. With a strong majority, the Cabinet dominates Parliament - Lord Hailsham called this 'elective dictatorship'. The 'shadow cabinet' of the opposition presents alternative policies.
The United States has a written federal constitution based on separation of powers and checks and balances.

The US Constitution was drafted at the Philadelphia Convention (1787) under George Washington's presidency, with James Madison called the 'father of the Constitution'; it came into force in 1789. It is the oldest written national constitution still in use, and very brief, with only seven articles. It has been amended only 27 times; the first ten amendments (1791) form the Bill of Rights. Amendment requires a two-thirds majority of both houses of Congress and ratification by three-fourths of states, making it very rigid.

Features: written and rigid; federal (power divided between national and state governments); presidential system; separation of powers (Article I - Congress; Article II - President; Article III - judiciary) with checks and balances; judicial review; Bill of Rights; republicanism; and popular sovereignty ('We the People'). The Federalist Papers (Madison, Hamilton and Jay) explained and defended the Constitution. Important amendments include the 13th (abolition of slavery, 1865), 14th (equal protection, 1868), 15th (voting regardless of race), 19th (women's suffrage, 1920) and 26th (voting age 18, 1971).
The President is both head of state and head of government and exercises important executive powers.

The US President is elected for four years through the Electoral College (538 electors; a candidate needs 270), with each state having electors equal to its members of Congress; most states give all their electors to the winner of the state's popular vote, so a candidate can win the presidency while losing the national popular vote (as in 2000 and 2016). Qualifications: natural-born citizen, at least 35 years old, resident for 14 years. The 22nd Amendment (1951) limits presidents to two terms.

Powers: chief executive (enforces laws, appoints officials and judges with the Senate's consent, issues executive orders); commander-in-chief of the armed forces; chief diplomat (makes treaties with the Senate's two-thirds approval, receives ambassadors); legislative role (State of the Union address, veto power - Congress can override by a two-thirds majority in both houses; 'pocket veto'); and judicial (pardons). Checks: Congress controls funds and can impeach (the House impeaches, the Senate tries; three presidents - Andrew Johnson, Bill Clinton and Donald Trump (twice) - were impeached but none was convicted; Nixon resigned in 1974). The President has become very powerful, described by Arthur Schlesinger as the 'Imperial Presidency'.
Congress is the federal legislature and consists of the House of Representatives and Senate.

Congress (Article I) is bicameral. The House of Representatives has 435 members elected for two years from districts allocated according to population; the Speaker presides and is a powerful party leader. The Senate has 100 members (two from each state, regardless of population) elected for six years, with one-third elected every two years; the Vice-President presides. This compromise (the 'Great Compromise' or Connecticut Compromise of 1787) balanced the interests of large and small states.

Powers: making laws (both houses must pass bills), levying taxes and appropriating funds ('power of the purse'; revenue bills must originate in the House), declaring war, regulating commerce, approving appointments and treaties (Senate), impeachment (House impeaches, Senate tries) and overriding presidential vetoes (two-thirds of both houses). The Senate is considered one of the most powerful upper houses in the world. Committees play a central role in legislation. The 'filibuster' (prolonged debate) in the Senate can block bills unless 60 senators vote to end it.
The Supreme Court interprets the Constitution and exercises judicial review.

The US Supreme Court (Article III) has nine justices, including the Chief Justice, appointed by the President with the Senate's consent and serving for life ('during good behaviour'). It has original jurisdiction in limited cases (involving states and ambassadors) and appellate jurisdiction, selecting about 60-80 cases a year from thousands of petitions (writ of certiorari).

Its power of judicial review, established in Marbury v. Madison (1803), makes it the final interpreter of the Constitution. Landmark decisions: Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857, upholding slavery), Plessy v. Ferguson (1896, 'separate but equal'), Brown v. Board of Education (1954, ending school segregation), Miranda v. Arizona (1966), Roe v. Wade (1973, abortion rights - overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson Women's Health Organization in 2022), and Obergefell v. Hodges (2015, same-sex marriage). The Court has been described as 'a continuous constitutional convention'. Debates continue about the politicisation of appointments.
Separation of powers divides governmental authority among executive, legislative and judicial institutions.

Montesquieu ('The Spirit of the Laws', 1748), based on his reading of the British constitution, argued that liberty requires the separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers: 'When the legislative and executive powers are united in the same person, or in the same body of magistrates, there can be no liberty... Again, there is no liberty if the judiciary power be not separated from the legislative and executive.' Locke had earlier distinguished legislative and executive powers.

The US Constitution applies this principle most fully: Congress makes laws, the President executes them, and the courts interpret them; members of one branch cannot serve in another. In parliamentary systems (Britain, India), the executive and legislature are fused, though the judiciary is independent; India follows a 'functional separation' rather than strict separation. Critics argue that complete separation is impossible and could cause deadlock; hence it is combined with checks and balances.
Checks and balances allow institutions to limit and supervise one another so that power is not concentrated in a single branch.
